title: Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium

questions.title: Four Core Assumptions of Perfect Competition
questions.prompt_template: Which combination of market characteristics defines the canonical economic benchmark of perfect competition?

hints.text: Recall the four strict structural conditions listed at the start of Section 7.1.
Focus on seller size, product uniformity, buyer/seller knowledge, and long-run market access.

options_template.text: Many small buyers and sellers, identical (homogeneous) products, perfect information, and free entry and exit in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Perfect competition requires numerous small participants, homogeneous goods, perfect information on prices and quality, and zero barriers to long-run entry and exit.

options_template.text: A few large firms, slightly differentiated products, heavy brand advertising, and high startup capital requirements.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Oligopoly / Monopolistic Competition Confusion): Few large firms, product differentiation, and high entry barriers characterize imperfectly competitive markets rather than perfect competition.

options_template.text: Many small sellers, patented proprietary products, confidential price negotiations, and government licensing caps.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Barriers & Differentiation Error): Patents, hidden prices, and licensing caps violate homogeneous products, perfect information, and free entry.

options_template.text: One dominant price leader surrounded by smaller firms selling identical goods under strict price floors.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dominant-Firm Fallacy): Perfect competition excludes any single firm with market power to act as a price leader or any binding price floor.

questions.title: Why a Competitive Firm Is a Price Taker
questions.prompt_template: Why does an individual wheat farm in a perfectly competitive market neither raise its price above nor cut its price below the prevailing market price P*?

hints.text: Think about what happens to buyers if a single farm charges one penny above P*, and whether cutting price is necessary to sell more.
Because products are identical and each farm is tiny relative to the market, buyers switch immediately if price rises, while the farm can already sell its entire harvest at P*.

options_template.text: Raising price increases total revenue slightly, while cutting price is prohibited by agricultural marketing laws.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Power & Legal-Constraint Confusion): Competitive firms cannot raise price without losing all buyers, and price taking stems from market structure rather than legal bans.

options_template.text: Charging even one penny above P* causes buyers to switch instantly to rivals selling an identical product, while cutting price below P* sacrifices revenue unnecessarily because the firm can already sell all it wishes at P*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Homogeneous goods and tiny individual market share mean any price above P* yields zero sales, while selling at P* already absorbs any feasible output the firm supplies.

options_template.text: Market demand is perfectly inelastic, so consumers buy the exact same quantity from the farm regardless of its price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Elasticity Confusion): The individual competitive firm faces a perfectly elastic—not perfectly inelastic—demand curve.

options_template.text: The farm's fixed costs prevent it from changing prices during the harvest season.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Price-Rigidity Fallacy): Price taking is driven by horizontal firm demand in a market of identical substitutes, not by fixed costs.

questions.title: Equality of Price, Marginal Revenue, and Average Revenue
questions.prompt_template: For a perfectly competitive firm facing a constant market equilibrium price P*, which revenue identity holds at every positive output level q?

hints.text: Write Total Revenue as TR = P* × q and examine both revenue per unit (TR/q) and extra revenue per additional unit (ΔTR/Δq).
Because the firm does not have to lower its price on previous units to sell one more unit, each extra unit adds exactly P* to Total Revenue.

options_template.text: Marginal Revenue is strictly less than Price (MR < P*) because selling more units pushes down the market price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopoly Revenue Transfer Error): MR < P applies to price-setting firms facing downward-sloping demand, not to price-taking competitive firms.

options_template.text: Average Revenue exceeds Marginal Revenue (AR > MR) whenever Marginal Cost is rising.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Revenue Conflation): Rising Marginal Cost affects profit margins, not the firm's revenue identity where AR = TR/q = P* and MR = P*.

options_template.text: Price equals Marginal Revenue and Average Revenue (P* = MR = AR).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since TR = P* × q with constant P*, Average Revenue is TR/q = P* and Marginal Revenue is ΔTR/Δq = P*, yielding P* = MR = AR.

options_template.text: Marginal Revenue rises as output expands because Total Revenue grows proportionally with q.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-vs-Marginal Confusion): Total Revenue increases linearly with q, which means its slope—Marginal Revenue—is constant at P*, not rising.

questions.title: The Marginal Rule for Short-Run Profit Maximization
questions.prompt_template: Assuming a competitive firm operates above its shutdown threshold, why does producing where P* = MR = MC maximize short-run economic profit?

hints.text: Compare the extra revenue (MR) and extra cost (MC) of producing one additional unit when q is below q* versus above q*.
Expanding adds to profit whenever MR > MC and reduces profit whenever MC > MR.

options_template.text: At that output level, Total Revenue reaches its highest possible dollar value.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Maximization Fallacy): Profit maximization equates MR and MC; for a price taker, Total Revenue rises endlessly with q even after MC exceeds P* and erodes profit.

options_template.text: At that output level, Average Total Cost is always guaranteed to be at its lowest possible value.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Minimum-ATC Confounding): P* = MC only coincides with minimum ATC in long-run equilibrium; in the short run, P* can lie above or below min ATC.

options_template.text: At that output level, Total Cost equals Total Revenue so the firm avoids all losses.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Break-Even Confounding): Equating MR and MC maximizes profit (or minimizes loss); TR = TC is the break-even condition, not the general profit-maximization rule.

options_template.text: Every unit before q* adds more to revenue than to cost (MR > MC), while every unit beyond q* adds more to cost than to revenue (MC > MR), so profit peaks exactly where P* = MR = MC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Stopping where the extra revenue of the last unit equals its extra cost captures every profit-enhancing unit while avoiding every profit-reducing unit.

questions.title: Why Optimal Output Lies on the Rising Segment of MC
questions.prompt_template: If a competitive firm's U-shaped Marginal Cost curve intersects its horizontal price line P* twice—once while MC is falling and once while MC is rising—which intersection maximizes profit and why?

hints.text: Think about what happens to profit if you produce one more unit just past an intersection where MC is falling below P*.
Profit is maximized only when the second-order condition holds: MC must be upward-sloping so that additional units beyond q* have MC > P*.

options_template.text: The intersection on the upward-sloping segment of MC, because producing beyond it incurs MC > P* (reducing profit), whereas the downward-sloping intersection represents a local profit minimum.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When MC crosses P* from below (rising MC), prior units had MC < P* and subsequent units have MC > P*, confirming a profit maximum (d²π/dq² = −d(MC)/dq < 0).

options_template.text: The intersection on the downward-sloping segment of MC, because lower output always minimizes Total Cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Minimization Fallacy): Minimizing Total Cost does not maximize profit; past the downward-sloping intersection, MC falls below P*, meaning expanding output increases profit.

options_template.text: Both intersections yield the exact same maximum economic profit because P* = MC holds at each point.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (First-Order-Only Oversight): P* = MC is necessary but not sufficient; the downward-sloping crossing minimizes profit locally, whereas the upward-sloping crossing maximizes it.

options_template.text: Neither intersection, because a competitive firm always selects the output at the bottom of the MC curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Min-MC Fallacy): Producing at min MC leaves profitable units unproduced whenever P* exceeds min MC.

questions.title: Canonical Condition for a Short-Run Shutdown
questions.prompt_template: Under what exact price condition should a perfectly competitive firm temporarily shut down (produce q = 0) in the short run?

hints.text: Compare the firm's profit from operating (TR − VC − FC) against its profit from shutting down (−FC).
Fixed cost FC cancels from both sides, leaving a comparison between price P and Average Variable Cost.

options_template.text: Whenever market price falls below minimum Average Total Cost (P < min ATC).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shutdown-Exit Conflation): P < min ATC signals negative economic profit and triggers long-run exit, but in the short run the firm still stays open if P ≥ min AVC.

options_template.text: Whenever market price falls below minimum Average Variable Cost (P < min AVC).
options_template.feedback: Correct. If P < min AVC, then TR < VC at every positive output, meaning operating loses more money than shutting down and paying only sunk fixed costs (−FC).

options_template.text: Whenever Total Revenue falls below Total Fixed Cost (TR < FC).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Coverage Error): Whether TR exceeds FC is irrelevant to shutdown; what matters is whether TR covers Variable Cost (TR ≥ VC).

options_template.text: Whenever Marginal Cost exceeds Average Variable Cost (MC > AVC).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rising-AVC Misinterpretation): MC exceeds AVC everywhere along the upward-sloping portion of AVC, which includes the entire active short-run supply curve.

questions.title: Economic Logic of Operating While Losing Money
questions.prompt_template: Why does a rational competitive firm continue operating in the short run when market price lies strictly between minimum Average Variable Cost and minimum Average Total Cost (min AVC < P < min ATC)?

hints.text: Remember that in the short run, signed leases and loan payments are sunk fixed costs that must be paid even if q = 0.
Check what happens to the surplus of revenue over variable cost (TR − VC) when P > AVC.

options_template.text: Because keeping the business open eliminates all fixed costs from the firm's income statement.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Avoidable-Fixed-Cost Error): Fixed costs are sunk in the short run and remain payable whether the firm operates or shuts down.

options_template.text: Because operating guarantees that the firm earns positive accounting profit even though economic profit is negative.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Guaranteed-Accounting-Profit Fallacy): A firm with min AVC < P < min ATC can suffer both economic and accounting losses yet still minimize its loss by operating.

options_template.text: Because each unit sold covers its variable cost and contributes positive cash (P − AVC) toward unavoidable sunk fixed costs, yielding a smaller loss than shutting down.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When TR > VC, operating generates a positive contribution margin that offsets part of FC, so −FC < TR − VC − FC < 0.

options_template.text: Because producing positive output allows the firm to raise the market price back above ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Setting Fallacy): A competitive price taker cannot influence market price through its own production decision.

questions.title: Distinguishing Temporary Shutdown from Permanent Exit
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately contrasts a short-run shutdown with a long-run exit in a perfectly competitive market?

hints.text: Focus on the time horizon and on whether fixed costs such as leases and equipment loans are still paid.
Review the 'Clear It Up' distinction between closing ski lifts in July versus permanently selling off equipment and ending leases.

options_template.text: A shutdown is permanent and eliminates all costs, whereas exit is temporary and requires continuing lease payments.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Definition Reversal): Shutdown is temporary in the short run (fixed costs continue), while exit is permanent in the long run (all costs cease).

options_template.text: Both shutdown and exit occur whenever P < min ATC, differing only in whether the firm announces the closure publicly.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Threshold Conflation): Shutdown is governed by P < min AVC in the short run, whereas exit is governed by P < min ATC in the long run.

options_template.text: Shutdown applies only to firms with zero fixed costs, whereas exit applies only to firms with high fixed costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Structure Misconception): Both decisions apply to firms with fixed costs; the distinction depends on whether fixed costs are sunk (short run) or avoidable (long run).

options_template.text: A shutdown is a temporary short-run decision to produce q = 0 while still paying sunk fixed costs, whereas exit is a permanent long-run decision to leave the industry and eliminate all fixed and variable costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Shutting down halts output temporarily while overhead continues (P < min AVC); exiting liquidates commitments once contracts expire (P < min ATC).

questions.title: Defining the Competitive Firm's Short-Run Supply Curve
questions.prompt_template: Which curve or curve segment represents a perfectly competitive firm's short-run supply curve?

hints.text: Ask what quantity the firm supplies at every possible price P—both above and below the shutdown threshold.
Above min AVC, the firm chooses q where P = MC on the rising portion of MC; below min AVC, it supplies q = 0.

options_template.text: The upward-sloping portion of the firm's Marginal Cost (MC) curve lying at or above minimum Average Variable Cost (min AVC).
options_template.feedback: Correct. For any P ≥ min AVC, the firm supplies the quantity on its rising MC curve where P = MC; for any P < min AVC, it shuts down and supplies zero.

options_template.text: The entire Marginal Cost (MC) curve from q = 0 upward, including points below minimum Average Variable Cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shutdown-Omission Error): Below min AVC, the firm does not produce along MC; it shuts down (q = 0) to avoid losing more than fixed cost.

options_template.text: The upward-sloping portion of the firm's Average Total Cost (ATC) curve lying above minimum ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average-vs-Marginal Supply Confusion): Profit maximization equates P to MC, not to ATC, so ATC does not trace the firm's quantity supplied.

options_template.text: The horizontal market price line P* = MR extending across all output levels.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Curve Confusion): The horizontal P* = MR line is the firm's demand curve, not its supply curve.

questions.topic: Zero Economic Profit vs. Accounting Profit
questions.title: Meaning of Zero Economic Profit in Long-Run Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: When economists state that a perfectly competitive firm earns 'zero economic profit' in long-run equilibrium, what does this imply about the firm's owner?

hints.text: Distinguish explicit accounting costs from implicit opportunity costs such as forgone salary and forgone interest on invested savings.
Zero economic profit equals a normal accounting profit.

options_template.text: The owner's Total Revenue equals zero after paying workers and suppliers, forcing imminent bankruptcy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting-Economic Profit Conflation): Zero economic profit does not mean zero cash income; explicit bills are fully paid and the owner earns a positive normal accounting profit.

options_template.text: The owner covers all explicit expenses plus the full implicit opportunity cost of her time and invested capital, earning a normal accounting profit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Economic profit subtracts both explicit and implicit costs from Total Revenue, so π_econ = 0 means accounting profit exactly matches the owner's next-best alternative return.

options_template.text: The firm has zero fixed costs and zero variable costs in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Cost Misinterpretation): All costs become variable in the long run, but positive production still requires paying real labor, material, and capital costs.

options_template.text: The owner earns a higher rate of return than in any alternative occupation, preventing rivals from entering.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Above-Normal Return Error): Earning more than the next-best alternative is positive economic profit (π_econ > 0), which attracts new entrants.

questions.title: The Long-Run Equilibrium Triple Equality
questions.prompt_template: Which set of equalities characterizes every active firm in a perfectly competitive industry once long-run equilibrium is reached?

hints.text: Combine the profit-maximization condition (P = MR = MC) with the zero-economic-profit condition (P = ATC).
Remember that MC intersects ATC at exactly one point: the minimum of ATC.

options_template.text: P_LR = MR = MC = min AVC, with positive economic profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shutdown-Equilibrium Confusion): P = min AVC is the short-run shutdown threshold (where the firm suffers a loss equal to FC), not long-run equilibrium.

options_template.text: P_LR > MC = min ATC, with barriers blocking further entry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Markup-Power Error): In perfect competition, firms are price takers with P = MC; P > MC reflects market power rather than competitive equilibrium.

options_template.text: P_LR = MR = MC = min ATC, with zero economic profit and no incentive for entry or exit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Free entry and exit drive market price to min ATC, where P_LR = MR = MC = min ATC holds simultaneously and economic profit is zero.

options_template.text: P_LR = MR > MC = ATC, with steady net entry of new firms every year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Disequilibrium Confusion): If P = MR > MC, firms are not maximizing profit; and ongoing entry means the market has not reached long-run equilibrium.

questions.title: Defining Productive vs. Allocative Efficiency
questions.prompt_template: Long-run competitive equilibrium achieves both productive efficiency and allocative efficiency. Which pair of conditions correctly defines these two concepts?

hints.text: Link 'productive' to minimizing average resource cost per unit and 'allocative' to matching consumer marginal valuation to marginal cost.
Check which equality uses min ATC and which uses P = MC.

options_template.text: Productive efficiency means P = MC (consumers' marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost); allocative efficiency means P = min ATC (output is produced at lowest average cost).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Efficiency-Label Swap): You reversed the two definitions—producing at min ATC is productive efficiency, while equating P = MC is allocative efficiency.

options_template.text: Productive efficiency means maximizing total firm revenue; allocative efficiency means equalizing income across all consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Non-Standard Efficiency Definitions): Neither revenue maximization nor income equality defines productive or allocative efficiency in microeconomics.

options_template.text: Productive efficiency means producing at zero fixed cost; allocative efficiency means producing at minimum AVC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Threshold Confusion): Efficient scale occurs at minimum ATC (including all long-run capital costs), and allocative efficiency requires P = MC.

options_template.text: Productive efficiency means producing at minimum Average Total Cost (P_LR = min ATC); allocative efficiency means producing the quantity where price equals marginal cost (P_LR = MC).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Operating at min ATC minimizes society's resource cost per unit (productive efficiency), while P = MC ensures no mutually beneficial trades remain unexploited (allocative efficiency).

questions.title: Constant-Cost, Increasing-Cost, and Decreasing-Cost Industries
questions.prompt_template: What determines whether a competitive market's long-run industry supply curve (S_LR) is horizontal, upward-sloping, or downward-sloping?

hints.text: Consider what happens to firms' input prices—and therefore min ATC—when total industry output expands through entry.
Match unchanged input prices (constant-cost), rising specialized input prices (increasing-cost), and external economies lowering input prices (decreasing-cost).

options_template.text: How industry expansion affects input prices and each firm's minimum ATC: unchanged input prices yield a horizontal S_LR, rising input prices yield an upward-sloping S_LR, and falling input prices (external economies) yield a downward-sloping S_LR.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Long-run price always settles at the new min ATC; thus S_LR is horizontal in a constant-cost industry, upward-sloping in an increasing-cost industry, and downward-sloping in a decreasing-cost industry.

options_template.text: Whether individual firms experience diminishing marginal returns in the short run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run Returns Confusion): Diminishing marginal returns make every firm's short-run MC upward-sloping, even in a constant-cost or decreasing-cost industry.

options_template.text: Whether consumers have elastic, unit-elastic, or inelastic market demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Elasticity Conflation): The slope of the long-run supply curve depends on industry-wide cost conditions as firms enter, not on the elasticity of market demand.

options_template.text: Whether firms earn positive, zero, or negative economic profit in long-run equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Run Profit Misconception): Free entry and exit drive economic profit to zero in long-run equilibrium across all three industry cost structures.

questions.title: Side-by-Side Market Demand vs. Firm Demand
questions.prompt_template: In the standard side-by-side diagram of perfect competition (Figure 7.1), why does the left-hand Industry Market panel show a downward-sloping demand curve D while the right-hand Price-Taking Firm panel shows a horizontal line at P*?

hints.text: Compare the horizontal axis scale of Market Q (millions of units) to Firm Output q (a tiny individual share).
Lower prices are needed to induce consumers to buy millions of extra market units, whereas one small firm's output change is too tiny to move P*.

options_template.text: Because the Law of Demand applies to buyers in the industry panel, but buyers ignore prices when purchasing from an individual firm.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Buyer-Behavior Misinterpretation): Buyers are extremely price-sensitive toward any single firm—charging above P* drives firm sales to zero, which is why firm demand is horizontal.

options_template.text: Because market-wide quantity changes are large enough to move equilibrium price down along market demand, whereas a single small firm's output is a tiny fraction of the market and leaves P* unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The resolution is scale: market demand slopes downward across millions of units, while one small farm takes the resulting market price P* as fixed, creating a horizontal P* = MR line.

options_template.text: Because the industry panel plots short-run demand while the firm panel plots long-run supply.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Panel-Axis Misreading): Both panels depict the exact same short-run equilibrium; the right panel shows the individual firm's perfectly elastic demand curve at P*.

options_template.text: Because the firm's horizontal line represents its Average Fixed Cost rather than its demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve-Identity Confusion): Average Fixed Cost slopes downward (FC/q), whereas the horizontal line at P* is the firm's demand, Marginal Revenue, and Average Revenue curve.

questions.title: Identifying the Short-Run Economic Profit Rectangle
questions.prompt_template: On a competitive firm's short-run cost-and-revenue graph where market price P* exceeds ATC(q*) at the profit-maximizing output q* (where P* = MC), which geometric area equals the firm's total economic profit?

hints.text: Recall the factored profit formula: π = (P* − ATC(q*)) × q*.
Match the vertical height (price minus ATC evaluated at q*) and horizontal width (0 to q*) of the shaded rectangle.

options_template.text: The entire rectangle from the horizontal axis up to P* across width q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Revenue Area Error): The full rectangle P* × q* equals Total Revenue (TR), not economic profit, because it fails to subtract Total Cost.

options_template.text: The triangle bounded by the horizontal price line P*, the vertical axis, and the MC curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Producer-Surplus Conflation): The area between P* and MC above min AVC measures producer surplus (TR − VC), which differs from economic profit by fixed costs.

options_template.text: The rectangle of width q* whose top edge lies at P* and whose bottom edge lies at ATC(q*) directly below the P* = MC intersection.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Height [P* − ATC(q*)] gives profit per unit and width q* gives quantity sold, so the shaded rectangle area equals (P* − ATC(q*)) × q* = π.

options_template.text: The rectangle of width q* whose top edge lies at P* and whose bottom edge lies at minimum ATC, regardless of where q* occurs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong-ATC-Evaluation Point): Profit per unit must be measured using ATC evaluated at the actual chosen output q*, not at the minimum of the ATC curve (unless q* = q_LR).

questions.title: Effect of a Market Demand Surge on a Price-Taking Firm
questions.prompt_template: Starting from long-run competitive equilibrium, suppose consumer preferences shift strongly toward organic blueberries, shifting market demand rightward. What happens immediately on an individual grower's short-run diagram?

hints.text: Trace the change from the left-hand Industry panel (P* rises) over to the right-hand Firm panel.
Does the firm's MC curve shift, or does the firm move along its existing MC curve as its horizontal P = MR line shifts?

options_template.text: The firm's MC and ATC curves shift rightward, keeping price unchanged while output increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Shift Confusion): A shift in consumer demand does not change a firm's production technology or input costs, so MC and ATC stay fixed.

options_template.text: The firm's horizontal P = MR line shifts downward, forcing the firm to cut output and incur losses.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong-Direction Price Shift): A rightward shift in market demand raises equilibrium price P*, shifting the firm's horizontal demand line upward, not downward.

options_template.text: The firm's horizontal P = MR line stays fixed at min ATC because competitive firms are price takers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static-Price Misconception): Being a price taker means the firm cannot set P* itself, not that P* never changes when market demand shifts.

options_template.text: The firm's horizontal P = MR line shifts upward above min ATC; the firm moves upward along its rising MC curve to a higher q* and earns positive short-run economic profit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher market demand raises P*, lifting the firm's horizontal P = MR line so that the new P* = MC intersection occurs at a higher q* with P* > ATC(q*).

questions.topic: Short-Run Comparative Statics: Supply Shock Elsewhere
questions.title: Drought Elsewhere and an Unaffected Farmer's Graph
questions.prompt_template: A severe drought destroys grain harvests in competing regions, shifting the global grain supply curve leftward, while an Iowa corn farm's own weather and cost curves are completely unaffected. How does this appear on the Iowa farm's short-run diagram?

hints.text: First determine what a leftward shift of global market supply does to the equilibrium spot price P*.
Then shift the unaffected Iowa farm's horizontal P = MR line accordingly while holding its MC and ATC curves constant.

options_template.text: Global spot price P* rises, shifting the Iowa farm's horizontal P = MR line upward so the farm expands output along its unchanged MC curve and earns positive short-run economic profit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Reduced market supply raises P*; because the Iowa farm's own cost curves did not shift, it moves up along MC to a larger q* and captures positive short-run profit.

options_template.text: The Iowa farm's MC curve shifts upward even though its own input costs did not change, causing it to reduce output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Spillover Cost-Shift Error): Because the Iowa farm's weather and input prices are unaffected, its MC and ATC curves remain stationary.

options_template.text: Global spot price P* falls, shifting the Iowa farm's horizontal P = MR line below min AVC and triggering a shutdown.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Shift Price Inversion): A leftward shift in market supply creates a shortage at the old price, pushing equilibrium price up, not down.

options_template.text: The Iowa farm's demand curve rotates from horizontal to downward-sloping because global output is smaller.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Structure Shift Error): One small farm still represents a microscopic share of global grain supply and remains a price taker with a horizontal demand line.

questions.title: Graphical Geometry of Shutdown and Break-Even Points
questions.prompt_template: In a consistent competitive firm cost diagram (Figure 7.2), where does the Marginal Cost (MC) curve intersect the Average Variable Cost (AVC) and Average Total Cost (ATC) curves?

hints.text: Recall the mathematical relationship between marginal and average curves (also proved via the quotient rule in Section 7.2).
Check both the vertical height and the horizontal ordering of q_SD and q_BE.

options_template.text: MC intersects AVC at its maximum point and ATC at its minimum point.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Extremum Error): Both AVC and ATC are U-shaped curves with minima, not maxima, at their intersections with MC.

options_template.text: MC intersects AVC at its exact minimum (the shutdown point q_SD) and intersects ATC at its exact minimum (the break-even point q_BE), with q_SD < q_BE and min AVC < min ATC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rising MC pulls down both averages while below them and pulls them up once above them, cutting AVC at min AVC and then cutting ATC at min ATC at a larger output and higher cost.

options_template.text: MC intersects ATC before it intersects AVC, so the break-even output q_BE is smaller than the shutdown output q_SD.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Threshold Ordering Reversal): Because ATC = AFC + AVC and AFC falls with output, ATC continues falling past min AVC until rising AVC outweighs falling AFC, so q_SD < q_BE.

options_template.text: MC intersects AVC and ATC at the exact same output level q, separated vertically by Average Fixed Cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Simultaneous-Minimum Fallacy): At q_SD, AVC is flat while AFC is still falling, so ATC is still declining and has not yet reached its minimum.

questions.title: Mapping Market Price into the Three Short-Run Decision Zones
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a firm's cost diagram shows min AVC = $12 and min ATC = $22. If the competitive market price is P* = $17, in which decision zone does the firm operate and what is its optimal short-run action?

hints.text: Compare P* = $17 against both vertical thresholds: min AVC ($12) and min ATC ($22).
Since $12 < $17 < $22, check whether the firm earns profit, operates at a loss, or shuts down.

options_template.text: Profit Zone: produce where P* = MC and earn positive economic profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Break-Even Misread): Positive economic profit requires P* > min ATC ($22); at $17, price lies below every point on the ATC curve.

options_template.text: Shutdown Zone: produce q = 0 immediately to avoid paying fixed costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Premature Shutdown Fallacy): Shutdown occurs only when P* < min AVC ($12), and shutting down never eliminates sunk fixed costs in the short run.

options_template.text: Operate-at-Loss Zone: produce the positive output q* where P* = MC, earning a negative economic profit that is strictly smaller than fixed costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because min AVC ($12) ≤ P* ($17) < min ATC ($22), revenue covers all variable costs and contributes cash toward fixed costs, minimizing short-run loss.

options_template.text: Long-Run Equilibrium Zone: produce at q_BE where P* = min ATC and earn zero economic profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium Price Error): Zero economic profit occurs only when P* = min ATC ($22), not at $17.

questions.title: Reading Loss and Contribution Rectangles When Operating at a Loss
questions.prompt_template: On a firm's short-run cost diagram where min AVC < P* < min ATC and the firm produces q* (where P* = MC), what do the two vertical gaps [ATC(q*) − P*] and [P* − AVC(q*)] represent?

hints.text: Remember that ATC(q*) − AVC(q*) = AFC(q*), and compare price P* to both ATC(q*) and AVC(q*).
One gap measures how much the firm loses per unit; the other measures how much cash each unit contributes toward fixed costs.

options_template.text: [ATC(q*) − P*] is the economic profit per unit, and [P* − AVC(q*)] is the unavoidable fixed cost per unit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-and-AFC Error): Since ATC(q*) > P*, the firm incurs a loss per unit rather than a profit, and AFC(q*) equals ATC(q*) − AVC(q*), not P* − AVC(q*).

options_template.text: [ATC(q*) − P*] is Total Fixed Cost, and [P* − AVC(q*)] is Total Variable Cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-vs-Per-Unit Confusion): Vertical distances between average curves and price measure per-unit dollar amounts, not total dollar costs.

options_template.text: [ATC(q*) − P*] is the economic loss per unit, while [P* − AVC(q*)] is the per-unit contribution toward paying sunk fixed costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Multiplying [ATC(q*) − P*] by q* yields total economic loss, while multiplying [P* − AVC(q*)] by q* yields the cash generated above variable cost that reduces the loss below FC.

options_template.text: Both gaps represent deadweight loss created because the firm refuses to shut down.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Deadweight-Loss Misapplication): Operating where P* = MC > AVC is both privately loss-minimizing and socially efficient because marginal benefit (P*) equals marginal cost (MC).

questions.title: Why Rising MC Still Pulls ATC Downward to the Left of q_BE
questions.prompt_template: Between the minimum of MC and the minimum of ATC, the Marginal Cost curve is already sloping upward, yet the Average Total Cost curve is still sloping downward. What explains this graphical pattern?

hints.text: Compare the height of MC to the height of ATC rather than looking only at whether MC is rising or falling.
Recall the GPA analogy (or d(ATC)/dq = [MC − ATC]/q): an average falls whenever the marginal addition lies below the current average.

options_template.text: Because ATC is determined solely by Fixed Cost, which always decreases regardless of MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Variable-Cost Omission): ATC = AFC + AVC; eventually rising AVC overcomes falling AFC, causing ATC to turn upward once MC rises above ATC.

options_template.text: Because as long as MC lies below ATC (MC < ATC), each additional unit costs less than the existing average, pulling ATC downward even while MC itself is rising.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The sign of d(ATC)/dq = (MC − ATC)/q depends on whether MC < ATC, not on the slope of MC; thus ATC falls until rising MC catches up to and crosses ATC at min ATC.

options_template.text: Because ATC can only slope upward after price rises above min ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Cost Dependency Error): Cost curves (MC, AVC, ATC) depend strictly on technology and input prices, never on market price P*.

options_template.text: Because the diagram violates mathematical consistency; ATC must turn upward at the exact same output where MC turns upward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Conflation Fallacy): In a consistent cubic cost system, MC reaches its minimum strictly before both AVC and ATC reach their minima.

questions.topic: Fixed-Cost Shift in the Short Run
questions.title: Graphical Effect of Higher Fixed Rent on Short-Run Supply
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a competitive print shop's landlord raises its unavoidable monthly lease rent (a pure increase in fixed cost FC), while market price P* and variable input prices remain unchanged. How do the shop's short-run cost curves and optimal output q* change?

hints.text: Check which cost curves include Fixed Cost (FC) and which depend strictly on Variable Cost (VC).
Remember that optimal short-run output depends on P* = MC and the shutdown condition depends on min AVC.

options_template.text: ATC shifts upward, while MC and AVC do not shift; assuming the firm stays above min AVC, its profit-maximizing output q* and shutdown price remain unchanged, though short-run profit falls (or loss widens).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because FC does not vary with output, neither MC nor AVC changes; only ATC shifts up, shrinking economic profit without altering the short-run P* = MC output decision.

options_template.text: MC, AVC, and ATC all shift upward by the same vertical amount, causing the firm to cut q* immediately.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-as-Marginal Cost Error): Fixed costs have zero derivative with respect to output (dFC/dq = 0) and therefore never shift MC or AVC.

options_template.text: MC shifts downward so the firm expands q* to spread its higher fixed rent across more units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Spreading-Overhead Fallacy): Producing past P* = MC adds units whose MC > P*, which strictly worsens profit or increases losses despite lowering AFC.

options_template.text: AVC shifts upward while ATC remains unchanged, raising the shutdown price above P*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve-Component Reversal): Fixed rent enters ATC (via AFC = FC/q) and never enters AVC.

questions.topic: Variable-Cost Shift in the Short Run
questions.title: Graphical Effect of Higher Hourly Wages on Short-Run Firm Curves
questions.prompt_template: Suppose hourly wages for production workers (a variable input) rise across a competitive industry while market price P* is momentarily held fixed. How do an individual firm's curves and short-run quantity supplied respond?

hints.text: Determine which cost curves incorporate variable labor costs: MC, AVC, and ATC.
Trace the new intersection of the unchanged P* line with the shifted MC curve.

options_template.text: Only ATC shifts upward while MC stays fixed, leaving the firm's short-run quantity supplied unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Variable-as-Fixed Cost Error): Hourly production wages vary directly with output, so they raise MC and AVC as well as ATC.

options_template.text: MC, AVC, and ATC all shift upward; at the unchanged price P*, the firm's short-run supply curve shifts leftward/upward, optimal output q* decreases, and the shutdown price min AVC rises.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher variable input prices increase the marginal and average variable cost of every unit, shifting MC, AVC, and ATC upward, reducing q* at any given P*, and raising min AVC.

options_template.text: MC shifts downward while AVC shifts upward, expanding q* to cover higher payroll expenses.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Opposite-Shift Contradiction): Higher variable wages increase both the marginal cost of extra units and average variable cost in the same upward direction.

options_template.text: The firm's horizontal demand line P* = MR shifts upward automatically to pass 100% of the wage hike onto buyers before market supply adjusts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Plus Price-Setting Fallacy): A competitive price taker cannot unilaterally raise P*; market price only rises once aggregate industry supply shifts leftward.

questions.title: Graphical Adjustment to Positive Profits in a Constant-Cost Industry
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 7.3, a constant-cost competitive industry begins with positive short-run profits at P1 > min ATC. Which sequence accurately describes the graphical transition to long-run equilibrium?

hints.text: Trace how positive economic profits trigger entry in the left-hand Industry panel and how that feeds back into the right-hand Firm panel.
In a constant-cost industry, each firm's ATC and MC curves stay fixed during entry.

options_template.text: Market demand shifts leftward until price drops to min ATC, while each firm's ATC curve shifts upward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-vs-Supply Adjustment Error): Entry shifts industry supply rightward; it does not shift consumer demand leftward, and in a constant-cost industry ATC does not shift.

options_template.text: Industry supply shifts leftward from S1 to S2, pushing price higher until profits peak.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Entry-Direction Reversal): Positive profits attract new firms into the market, which expands (shifts rightward) industry supply and lowers price.

options_template.text: New firms enter, shifting industry supply rightward from S1 to S2; market quantity rises (Q1 → Q_LR) and price falls (P1 → P_LR = min ATC), lowering each firm's horizontal P = MR line until it is tangent to min ATC at q_LR.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rightward supply shifts drive P down to min ATC, moving each individual firm down along its MC curve to efficient scale q_LR with zero economic profit.

options_template.text: Existing firms expand their individual plants until each firm's MC curve becomes horizontal.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Plant-Expansion Confusion): Long-run industry expansion in a constant-cost competitive model occurs via entry of additional firms operating at efficient scale q_LR, not via flat firm MC curves.

questions.title: Graphical Adjustment to Short-Run Losses in a Constant-Cost Industry
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a permanent drop in demand pushes market price below min ATC in a constant-cost competitive industry, causing firms to incur short-run economic losses. How does the side-by-side diagram reach its new long-run equilibrium?

hints.text: Determine whether economic losses induce entry or exit when long-run leases expire.
Trace the resulting shift in market supply, market price, and surviving firms' horizontal P = MR lines.

options_template.text: Firms remain permanently at a loss because sunk fixed costs prevent exit in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Permanent-Sunk-Cost Fallacy): Fixed costs are sunk only in the short run; in the long run leases expire and all costs are avoidable, so money-losing firms exit.

options_template.text: Firms permanently exit, shifting industry supply leftward; total market quantity falls further while market price rises back to P_LR = min ATC, lifting surviving firms' P = MR lines back to tangency with min ATC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Exit shrinks industry supply, raising price until surviving firms break even at P_LR = min ATC with zero economic profit and fewer total firms in the market.

options_template.text: New firms enter to buy discounted equipment, shifting industry supply rightward and pushing price down to min AVC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Counter-Profit Entry Error): Negative economic profits deter entry and trigger exit; industry price rises rather than falling to min AVC.

options_template.text: Surviving firms shift their ATC curves downward until min ATC matches the depressed short-run price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Endogenous Cost-Cut Fallacy): In a constant-cost industry, input prices and firm cost curves do not shift; equilibrium is restored by supply contraction raising market price.

questions.title: Tracing an Upward-Sloping S_LR Curve in an Increasing-Cost Industry
questions.prompt_template: Starting from long-run equilibrium in an increasing-cost competitive industry, a permanent surge in demand raises short-run price and attracts new entrants. Why does the new long-run equilibrium price settle above the original P_LR, tracing an upward-sloping S_LR curve?

hints.text: Think about what happens to scarce, specialized input prices as more firms enter and expand industry output.
Show how higher input prices move each firm's ATC and MC curves vertically while entry moves industry supply rightward.

options_template.text: Because entry bids up the prices of scarce specialized inputs, shifting every firm's MC and ATC curves upward so that the new zero-profit point (min ATC) lies at a higher price than before.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Although entry shifts market supply rightward and brings price down from its short-run peak, rising input prices lift min ATC, leaving the new long-run price permanently higher and S_LR upward-sloping.

options_template.text: Because entry stops while firms are still earning positive economic profits in an increasing-cost industry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Persistent-Profit Error): Free entry continues until economic profit is zero in all competitive industries; price stays higher because min ATC itself rose.

options_template.text: Because market demand shifts leftward after new firms enter.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Reversal Confusion): Entry shifts supply, not demand; and a leftward demand shift would push price down rather than keep it higher.

options_template.text: Because firms in an increasing-cost industry act as monopolies once industry output grows.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Structure Drift Error): Firms remain small price takers; the upward slope of S_LR reflects rising industry-wide factor prices, not monopoly pricing.

questions.title: Solving for Optimal Output q* Using P* = MC
questions.prompt_template: A competitive strawberry grower faces a market price of P* = $38 per flat. The grower's cost schedules are TC(q) = 60 + 10q + 2q^2, AVC(q) = 10 + 2q, and MC(q) = 10 + 4q. What is the grower's profit-maximizing quantity q*?

hints.text: Apply the competitive profit-maximization rule P* = MC(q*) and solve the linear equation for q*.
Set 38 = 10 + 4q*, solve for q*, and verify that P* exceeds AVC(q*) so the firm does not shut down.

options_template.text: 7 flats
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting P* = MC gives 38 = 10 + 4q* → 28 = 4q* → q* = 7 flats. Checking shutdown: AVC(7) = 10 + 2(7) = $24 < $38, so producing 7 flats maximizes profit.

options_template.text: 14 flats
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (P = AVC Substitution Error): Solving 38 = 10 + 2q yields 14 flats, which equates price to Average Variable Cost instead of Marginal Cost.

options_template.text: 12 flats
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-Inversion Algebra Error): Adding 10 instead of subtracting 10 gives (38 + 10)/4 = 12 flats; you must subtract 10 from 38 before dividing by 4.

options_template.text: 9.5 flats
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dropped-Intercept Error): Dividing 38 directly by 4 gives 9.5 flats by omitting the +10 constant term in MC(q) = 10 + 4q.

questions.title: Calculating Short-Run Economic Profit from TC(q) and MC(q)
questions.prompt_template: A price-taking honey producer sells jars at P* = $44 per crate. Its cost schedules are TC(q) = 75 + 8q + 3q^2, AVC(q) = 8 + 3q, and MC(q) = 8 + 6q. What is the producer's maximum short-run economic profit?

hints.text: Step 1: Find q* by setting P* = MC(q*). Step 2: Compute TR = P* × q* and TC(q*).
Solve 44 = 8 + 6q* for q*, then substitute q* into TC(q) = 75 + 8q + 3q^2 (do not forget the $75 fixed cost) and compute π = TR − TC.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Fixed Cost Error): $108 equals TR − VC ($264 − $156), which omits the $75 fixed cost in TC(q) = 75 + 8q + 3q^2.
Correct. Setting 44 = 8 + 6q* yields q* = 6 crates (with AVC(6) = $26 < $44). At q* = 6, TR = $44 × 6 = $264 and TC(6) = 75 + 48 + 108 = $231, giving π = $264 − $231 = +$33.
Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-as-Profit Error): $264 is Total Revenue ($44 × 6); economic profit requires subtracting Total Cost ($231).
Diagnostic fallacy (P = AVC Quantity Error): Setting 44 = 8 + 3q gives q = 12, where TR = $528 and TC = $603 (profit = −$75); profit maximization requires P* = MC, not P* = AVC.

questions.title: Computing Economic Profit via the Profit-Rectangle Formula
questions.prompt_template: At its profit-maximizing output of q* = 40 crates per week (where P* = MC), a competitive orchard faces a market price of P* = $25.00 per crate and has Average Total Cost ATC(40) = $21.50 per crate. What is the orchard's weekly economic profit?

hints.text: Use the factored profit-rectangle formula: π = (P* − ATC(q*)) × q*.
First find profit per crate ($25.00 − $21.50), then multiply by all 40 crates.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Per-Unit-Only Error): $3.50 is the economic profit per crate (P* − ATC); you must multiply by q* = 40 crates to obtain total weekly economic profit.
Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Revenue Substitution): $1,000.00 is Total Revenue ($25.00 × 40), before subtracting Total Cost ($860.00).
Correct. Profit per crate is $25.00 − $21.50 = $3.50, and multiplying by q* = 40 yields π = $3.50 × 40 = +$140.00 (cross-check: TR $1,000 − TC $860 = +$140).
Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Cost Substitution): $860.00 is Total Cost ($21.50 × 40), not economic profit.

questions.title: Comparing Operating Loss vs. Shutdown Loss for a Bakery
questions.prompt_template: A competitive neighborhood bakery pays unavoidable daily fixed rent of FC = $450. During a slow week, market price drops to P = $12 per loaf. At its loss-minimizing output of q* = 60 loaves per day (where P = MC), Total Variable Cost is VC = $540 (so AVC = $9 and ATC = $16.50). What is the bakery's optimal short-run profit/loss and decision?

hints.text: Calculate both π_operate = TR − (FC + VC) and π_shutdown = −FC, then compare the two losses.
TR = $12 × 60 = $720 and TC = $450 + $540 = $990; compare that deficit to losing $450 by shutting down.

options_template.text: Shut down immediately, because operating loses $990 per day whereas shutting down loses $450.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Cost-as-Loss Error): $990 is Total Cost before crediting $720 in Total Revenue; the net operating loss is only $270, not $990.

options_template.text: Shut down immediately, because P ($12) < ATC ($16.50) means any positive output causes a loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Run Exit Misapplied to Short Run): Although P < ATC means the bakery loses money, P ($12) > AVC ($9) means operating shrinks the daily loss by $180 compared to shutting down.

options_template.text: Stay open in the short run and earn a positive profit of +$180 per day.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Fixed Cost Error): +$180 is the contribution margin (TR − VC = $720 − $540), which offsets part of the $450 fixed rent but still leaves a net loss of −$270.

options_template.text: Stay open in the short run, incurring a daily loss of −$270 instead of a shutdown loss of −$450.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Operating yields TR = $720 and TC = $990 (π_operate = −$270), whereas shutting down yields π_shutdown = −$450; staying open saves $180 per day toward fixed rent.

questions.title: Identifying When Shutting Down Minimizes Short-Run Loss
questions.prompt_template: A competitive café pays daily fixed costs of FC = $500. During an off-season slump, market price falls to P = $7 per meal. At the output where P = MC (q* = 80 meals), Total Variable Cost is VC = $640 (so AVC = $8). How much money does the café save per day by shutting down (q = 0) instead of operating at q* = 80?

hints.text: Compute π_operate = TR − (FC + VC) and compare it to π_shutdown = −FC.
Check the per-meal shortfall (AVC − P = $8 − $7 = $1) multiplied by 80 meals.

options_template.text: $80 saved per day (losing $500 by shutting down instead of $580 by operating).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Operating yields TR = $560 and TC = $500 + $640 = $1,140 (loss of $580), whereas shutting down loses only FC = $500; shutting down avoids the $80 variable-cost deficit.

options_template.text: $500 saved per day (eliminating fixed rent by closing the doors).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Avoidable-Fixed-Cost Fallacy): In the short run, FC = $500 is sunk and must still be paid when q = 0; shutting down only avoids the $80 loss on variable costs.

options_template.text: $560 lost by shutting down, so the café should stay open to collect $560 in daily revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Without-VC Fallacy): Collecting $560 in revenue requires spending $640 on variable inputs, making the café $80 worse off than shutting down.

options_template.text: $640 saved per day because shutting down eliminates Total Variable Cost with no revenue loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored-Revenue Error): Shutting down avoids $640 in variable costs, but it also gives up $560 in revenue, for a net savings of $640 − $560 = $80.

questions.title: Finding the Exact Shutdown Price Where MC = AVC
questions.prompt_template: A competitive manufacturer has Average Variable Cost AVC(q) = 24 − 4q + 0.5q^2 and Marginal Cost MC(q) = 24 − 8q + 1.5q^2 for q > 0. What is the firm's exact short-run shutdown price (min AVC)?

hints.text: Recall that Marginal Cost intersects Average Variable Cost at its exact minimum (MC(q_SD) = AVC(q_SD)).
Set 24 − 8q + 1.5q^2 = 24 − 4q + 0.5q^2 to solve for q_SD > 0, then substitute q_SD back into AVC(q).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Vertical-Intercept Error): $24 is AVC(0) at the vertical intercept, not the minimum of the U-shaped AVC curve, which dips below $24 as q rises to 4.
Correct. Setting MC = AVC gives 24 − 8q + 1.5q^2 = 24 − 4q + 0.5q^2 → q^2 = 4q → q_SD = 4. Substituting q_SD = 4 yields min AVC = 24 − 4(4) + 0.5(16) = 24 − 16 + 8 = $16.
Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-Price Substitution Error): 4 is the shutdown output quantity q_SD; you must substitute q_SD = 4 into AVC(q) to obtain the shutdown price in dollars ($16).

Diagnostic fallacy (Factor-of-Two Algebra Error): Solving incorrectly for q = 2 and evaluating AVC(2) = 24 − 8 + 2 gives $18; correctly simplifying 1.5q^2 − 0.5q^2 = 8q − 4q gives q^2 = 4q, so q_SD = 4.

questions.topic: Solving for Efficient Scale and Long-Run Price
questions.title: Finding Break-Even Price (min ATC) via MC = ATC
questions.prompt_template: Each firm in a constant-cost competitive industry has Total Cost TC(q) = 144 + 16q + q^2, giving Average Total Cost ATC(q) = 144/q + 16 + q and Marginal Cost MC(q) = 16 + 2q. What is the long-run equilibrium market price P_LR?

hints.text: In long-run equilibrium, P_LR = min ATC, which occurs at the efficient scale q_LR where MC(q) = ATC(q).
Set 16 + 2q = 144/q + 16 + q, solve for q_LR > 0, and substitute q_LR into MC(q) (or ATC(q)).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-as-Price Error): 12 is the efficient-scale output q_LR (since q^2 = 144 → q_LR = 12); substitute q_LR = 12 into MC = 16 + 2q to obtain the dollar price.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted-AFC Error): $28 equals 16 + 12, omitting the Average Fixed Cost term 144/12 = $12 (or using AVC instead of ATC).
Correct. Setting MC = ATC gives 16 + 2q = 144/q + 16 + q → q = 144/q → q^2 = 144 → q_LR = 12. Plugging q_LR = 12 into MC(12) = 16 + 2(12) (or ATC(12) = 12 + 16 + 12) gives P_LR = $40.
Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counted AFC Error): Adding 144/12 ($12) onto MC(12) ($40) double-counts fixed cost, yielding $52 instead of $40.

questions.title: Aggregating Short-Run Output Across Identical Competitive Firms
questions.prompt_template: A competitive regional wheat market consists of 80 identical farms, each with Marginal Cost MC(q) = 4 + 0.5q and shutdown price min AVC = $6 per bushel. At a market price of P = $14 per bushel, what is the total short-run industry quantity supplied Q_S?

hints.text: First check that P ≥ min AVC, then solve P = MC(q*) for one farm's output q*.
Once you find q* from 14 = 4 + 0.5q*, horizontally sum across all 80 identical farms (Q_S = 80 × q*).

options_template.text: 20 bushels
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Firm Output Error): 20 bushels is the optimal output of one farm; total industry supply multiplies by all 80 identical farms.

options_template.text: 2,240 bushels
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dropped-Intercept Error): Ignoring the +4 constant in MC(q) = 4 + 0.5q yields q = 14/0.5 = 28 per farm and 80 × 28 = 2,240 bushels.

options_template.text: 400 bushels
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplication-for-Division Error): Multiplying (14 − 4) by 0.5 instead of dividing by 0.5 gives q = 5 per farm and 80 × 5 = 400 bushels.

options_template.text: 1,600 bushels
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since P = $14 > min AVC = $6, each farm operates where 14 = 4 + 0.5q* → 10 = 0.5q* → q* = 20 bushels. Across 80 identical farms, Q_S = 80 × 20 = 1,600 bushels.

questions.topic: Long-Run Industry Equilibrium Number of Firms
questions.title: Calculating Market Quantity and Equilibrium Firm Count N*
questions.prompt_template: In a constant-cost competitive dog-grooming industry, every identical shop achieves minimum Average Total Cost of min ATC = $30 per appointment at its efficient scale of q_LR = 20 appointments per week. Weekly market demand is Q_d = 1,800 − 20P. How many shops operate in long-run equilibrium (N*)?

hints.text: Step 1: Set P_LR = min ATC = $30 and substitute into Q_d = 1,800 − 20P to find Q_LR.
Step 2: Divide total market output Q_LR by each shop's efficient scale q_LR = 20 using N* = Q_LR / q_LR.

options_template.text: 60 shops
options_template.feedback: Correct. Long-run price equals min ATC = $30, so Q_LR = 1,800 − 20(30) = 1,200 appointments per week. Dividing by q_LR = 20 yields N* = 1,200 / 20 = 60 shops.

options_template.text: 40 shops
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Divisor Error): Dividing Q_LR = 1,200 by P_LR = $30 gives 40; you must divide total market quantity by each firm's output q_LR = 20, not by price.

options_template.text: 90 shops
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Intercept Error): Dividing the horizontal demand intercept 1,800 by q_LR = 20 ignores the price term −20P at P_LR = $30.

options_template.text: 120 shops
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-Inversion Demand Error): Adding 20(30) instead of subtracting gives Q = 2,400 and N = 2,400 / 20 = 120; downward-sloping demand requires subtracting 20P.

questions.topic: Long-Run Entry After a Permanent Demand Shift
questions.title: Calculating Net Entry (ΔN) in a Constant-Cost Industry
questions.prompt_template: A constant-cost competitive bicycle-tune-up industry has identical shops with min ATC = $25 at efficient scale q_LR = 15 tune-ups per week. Initially, market demand is Q_d1 = 1,400 − 20P. After new bike lanes open, demand shifts permanently to Q_d2 = 1,700 − 20P. How many net new shops enter the industry between the initial and new long-run equilibria?

hints.text: Because this is a constant-cost industry, long-run equilibrium price remains P_LR = $25 before and after the demand shift.
Calculate Q_1 and N_1 = Q_1 / 15, then Q_2 and N_2 = Q_2 / 15, and subtract ΔN = N_2 − N_1.

options_template.text: 80 new shops
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-vs-Change Error): 80 is the new total number of shops in the industry (N_2 = 1,200 / 15); subtracting the initial 60 shops gives 20 net new entrants.

options_template.text: 20 new shops
300 new shops
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-as-Firm-Count Error): 300 is the increase in weekly market tune-ups (ΔQ = 1,200 − 900), not the number of new shops; divide by q_LR = 15.

options_template.text: 12 new shops
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Divisor Error): Dividing ΔQ = 300 by P_LR = $25 gives 12; firm entry divides ΔQ by each firm's efficient scale q_LR = 15.

questions.title: Computing Accounting Profit and Economic Profit for a Food Truck
questions.prompt_template: A competitive food-truck owner earns $240,000 in annual revenue and pays $165,000 in explicit food, fuel, staff, and permit expenses. By running the truck, she forgoes a $65,000 chef salary and $10,000 in annual interest on personal savings invested in the truck. What are her accounting profit and economic profit, respectively?

hints.text: Accounting profit subtracts only explicit costs from Total Revenue.
Economic profit subtracts both explicit costs and all implicit opportunity costs (forgone salary plus forgone interest).

options_template.text: Accounting profit = $75,000; economic profit = $10,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Capital Opportunity Cost): Subtracting only the $65,000 forgone salary leaves out the $10,000 implicit interest cost on invested savings.

options_template.text: Accounting profit = $75,000; economic profit = $75,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted All Implicit Costs): Treating accounting profit as economic profit ignores both the $65,000 forgone salary and the $10,000 forgone interest.

options_template.text: Accounting profit = $75,000; economic profit = $0.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Accounting profit is $240,000 − $165,000 = $75,000. Subtracting total implicit costs ($65,000 + $10,000 = $75,000) yields $0 economic profit—a normal return in long-run equilibrium.

options_template.text: Accounting profit = $65,000; economic profit = −$10,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Implicit-in-Accounting Error): Forgone interest ($10,000) is an implicit opportunity cost, not an explicit accounting expense, so it should not be subtracted from accounting profit.

questions.title: Finding Profit-Maximizing Output from a Discrete Cost Schedule
questions.prompt_template: A competitive flower grower sells bouquets at a fixed market price of P* = $18 per bouquet. Total Cost across integer quantities is: TC(0) = $10, TC(1) = $20, TC(2) = $32, TC(3) = $46, TC(4) = $62, TC(5) = $84, and TC(6) = $110. What quantity maximizes short-run economic profit, and what is that maximum profit?

hints.text: Compute Marginal Cost MC(q) = TC(q) − TC(q − 1) for each unit and keep expanding as long as P* > MC.
Compare MC(4) = $62 − $46 = $16 against MC(5) = $84 − $62 = $22, then compute π = (18 × q*) − TC(q*).

options_template.text: q* = 5 bouquets, with maximum profit = +$6.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overproduction Past P = MC): The 5th bouquet adds $22 to cost (TC rises from $62 to $84) but only $18 to revenue, reducing profit from +$10 down to +$6.

options_template.text: q* = 3 bouquets, with maximum profit = +$8.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Premature Stopping Error): Stopping at 3 bouquets leaves profitable output on the table because the 4th bouquet adds $16 in cost while bringing in $18 in revenue (+$2 profit).

options_template.text: q* = 6 bouquets, with maximum profit = +$108.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Revenue Maximization Error): $108 is Total Revenue at q = 6; subtracting TC(6) = $110 actually yields a loss of −$2.

options_template.text: q* = 4 bouquets, with maximum profit = +$10.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Marginal Costs are $10, $12, $14, $16, $22, and $26. Producing through q* = 4 captures every unit with MC < $18 and stops before MC(5) = $22 > $18, yielding π = ($18 × 4) − $62 = +$10.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating the Food-Truck Boom and Cooling Profits
questions.prompt_template: In the chapter's gourmet food-truck case study, early operators earned large economic profits, yet within two years most trucks reported 'barely breaking even' while continuing to operate. Which economic explanation best accounts for this trajectory?

hints.text: Connect modest startup barriers to long-run entry dynamics in Section 7.3.
Remember why 'barely breaking even' in economic terms still keeps operators happily in business.

options_template.text: Modest startup barriers allowed new food trucks to enter while P > min ATC, shifting market supply rightward until price settled at P_LR = min ATC where trucks earn zero economic profit (a full normal accounting return).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Free entry acts as a self-correcting thermostat: entry compresses prices to min ATC, eliminating above-normal economic profits while still paying owners their full opportunity cost.

options_template.text: Consumers grew permanently tired of food trucks, causing every truck to operate below min AVC without realizing it.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Collapse Assumption): Profits erode in open competitive markets even when consumer demand remains strong, purely through supply expansion from new entrants.

options_template.text: Surviving trucks remained open only because of the sunk-cost fallacy, since rational owners always exit once economic profit reaches zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Economic-Profit Misinterpretation): Zero economic profit means owners earn a normal accounting profit matching their next-best alternative, so staying open is completely rational.

options_template.text: Early trucks raised prices too high and drove away customers before competitors arrived.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Setter Attribution): In an open, competitive street-food market, early profits reflect strong demand relative to initial supply rather than unilateral monopoly pricing.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Comparing a Winter Beachfront Hotel to a Summer Ski Resort
questions.prompt_template: During off-peak seasons, a beachfront hotel stays open at $95/night (below its full average total cost, with housekeeping and utility AVC = $45/night), while a mountain ski resort closes its chairlifts in July while continuing to pay property taxes and loan installments. How does the competitive model explain both choices simultaneously?

hints.text: Apply the exact same short-run decision rule (compare off-peak P to min AVC) to both businesses.
Notice that both firms pay sunk fixed overhead off-season, so the decisive difference is whether off-season revenue covers variable operating costs.

options_template.text: The hotel is ignoring its long-run exit rule, whereas the ski resort has permanently exited the recreation industry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Seasonal-as-Permanent Confusion): Seasonal dips are short-run fluctuations; the ski resort is temporarily shutting down in July, not permanently exiting the industry.

options_template.text: Both firms apply the identical short-run shutdown rule: the hotel's off-peak price ($95) exceeds AVC ($45), contributing $50/night toward fixed mortgage costs, whereas the ski resort's July lift revenue would fall below variable operating costs (P < min AVC).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Comparing P to min AVC explains both behaviors cleanly: operating shrinks the hotel's short-run loss, while temporary shutdown minimizes the ski resort's summer loss.

options_template.text: Hotels have zero fixed costs in autumn, while ski resorts have zero fixed costs in summer.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Fixed-Cost Misconception): Both businesses carry substantial fixed mortgages, insurance, and property taxes year-round.

options_template.text: The hotel maximizes Total Revenue regardless of cost, while the ski resort maximizes Average Total Cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Objective-Function Error): Both firms are minimizing short-run losses (maximizing profit) by comparing marginal and variable revenues against variable costs.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Diagnosing the Sunk-Cost Fallacy in a Failing Restaurant
questions.prompt_template: A restaurant owner in a competitive dining district argues: 'I already signed a nonrefundable $60,000 annual lease. Even though slow winter weekday lunches bring in less cash than the hourly wages and ingredients needed to stay open, I must keep serving lunch so my rent money isn't wasted.' How should an economist evaluate this reasoning?

hints.text: Identify which cost is sunk in the short run ($60,000 lease) and check the inequality between lunch revenue and variable costs (TR vs. VC).
Ask whether staying open for weekday lunches reduces the $60,000 loss or adds an extra variable-cost deficit on top of it.

options_template.text: The owner is correct, because shutting down during weekday lunches guarantees a 100% loss on the lease.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk-Cost Fallacy Endorsement): The lease payment is unavoidable either way; operating when TR < VC adds extra losses on top of the $60,000 lease.

options_template.text: The owner is correct only if Total Revenue exceeds the $60,000 lease payment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Benchmark Error): The relevant short-run threshold is whether weekday lunch revenue covers weekday variable costs (TR ≥ VC), not whether it covers the annual lease.

options_template.text: The owner is committing the sunk-cost fallacy: because the lease is sunk, serving lunch when TR < VC (P < AVC) increases total losses beyond $60,000, so temporarily closing for winter weekday lunches minimizes losses.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Sunk fixed rent should not drive short-run operating hours; whenever lunch revenue fails to cover variable food and labor costs, shutting down during those hours strictly saves money.

options_template.text: The owner should double lunch output to push Average Fixed Cost down below menu prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Volume-Fixes-Deficit Fallacy): When price does not even cover Average Variable Cost, selling more meals compounds the variable-cost deficit on every extra plate.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Policy Incidence: Lump-Sum Fee vs. Per-Unit Tax
questions.title: Comparing a Fixed Annual License Fee to a Per-Unit Tax
questions.prompt_template: A city council is choosing between two policies for a constant-cost competitive market initially in long-run equilibrium: (Policy A) a flat annual lump-sum operating license fee per firm, or (Policy B) a per-unit excise tax on every unit sold. How do their immediate short-run effects and long-run price effects compare?

hints.text: Classify the lump-sum fee as a fixed cost (shifts ATC only) and the per-unit tax as a variable/marginal cost (shifts MC, AVC, and ATC).
Remember that in the long run, ANY increase in min ATC causes exit until P_LR rises to the new min ATC.

options_template.text: Policy A raises neither short-run nor long-run equilibrium price because fixed costs never affect competitive markets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run-Only Extrapolation): While a lump-sum fee leaves short-run MC and output unchanged, it raises min ATC, causing economic losses and long-run exit that raises P_LR.

options_template.text: Policy A leaves short-run MC and firm output unchanged while creating losses that trigger long-run exit and a higher P_LR; Policy B immediately shifts short-run MC upward (cutting output and raising price right away) and also raises P_LR in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A flat license fee affects only ATC in the short run (no immediate supply shift) but pushes P_LR up via long-run exit; a per-unit tax shifts MC immediately in the short run and raises min ATC in the long run.

options_template.text: Policy B shifts only ATC without changing MC, whereas Policy A shifts MC upward immediately.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Classification Reversal): A per-unit tax varies directly with output (shifting MC), whereas a flat annual fee is fixed regardless of output (shifting only ATC).

options_template.text: Neither policy changes long-run market price because free entry always keeps P_LR at its original pre-tax level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Invariant-Price Misconception): Free entry drives price to each firm's post-tax min ATC, which is strictly higher under both policies.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Long-Run Beneficiaries of a Per-Unit Competitive Subsidy
questions.prompt_template: Suppose the government grants a permanent $5 per-unit production subsidy to all growers in a constant-cost competitive vegetable market initially in long-run equilibrium. Once free entry fully adjusts in the long run, who captures the economic benefit of the $5 subsidy?

hints.text: Trace how a $5 per-unit subsidy shifts every firm's net MC and net ATC downward by $5.
In a constant-cost industry, where does P_LR settle after entry eliminates short-run economic profits?

options_template.text: Growers permanently keep the entire $5 per unit as positive economic profit while consumer prices stay unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static-Profit Illusion): Growers earn positive profits only in the short run; free entry shifts industry supply rightward until economic profit returns to zero.

options_template.text: Consumers capture the full $5 per-unit benefit through a $5 drop in the long-run equilibrium price, while growers expand total market volume and return to zero economic profit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The subsidy lowers every firm's net min ATC by $5; free entry shifts market supply rightward until P_LR falls by the full $5, returning growers to normal accounting profit.

options_template.text: Market quantity falls because growers produce less once they receive government support.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Shift Inversion): Lower net MC and net ATC induce both short-run expansion and long-run entry, strictly increasing equilibrium quantity.

options_template.text: Neither consumers nor growers benefit because the subsidy shifts market demand leftward by $5.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Demand Confusion): A production subsidy lowers sellers' net cost curves (supply), not consumers' willingness to pay (demand).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Welfare Effects of Municipal Caps on Competitive Permits
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a city responds to incumbent complaints about crowded streets by freezing the total number of food-truck permits permanently while consumer demand for food-truck lunches grows rapidly. Using the competitive model, what is the long-run consequence of this permit cap?

hints.text: Ask which assumption of perfect competition is broken when a city freezes the number of permits.
Compare the resulting price and output against the long-run competitive benchmarks P = min ATC and P = MC.

options_template.text: The permit cap guarantees productive and allocative efficiency by keeping food-truck owners profitable.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Profit-as-Efficiency Fallacy): Efficiency requires P = MC = min ATC; blocking entry restricts total output, keeps price above min ATC, and forces incumbents past efficient scale.

options_template.text: Blocking free entry prevents market supply from shifting rightward, leaving price persistently above min ATC, preserving positive economic profits (rents) for permit holders, and reducing consumer surplus and total efficiency.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Without free entry, rising demand cannot be accommodated by new trucks at min ATC; prices stay elevated, incumbent permit holders capture rents, and market output stays below the efficient level.

options_template.text: Market price still falls back to min ATC automatically because incumbent trucks cannot charge above min ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic-Zero-Profit Fallacy): Zero economic profit depends critically on free entry; when entry is legally blocked, market equilibrium price remains above min ATC.

options_template.text: Incumbent food trucks suffer economic losses because the permit cap shifts consumer demand leftward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Barrier-Direction Error): Limiting the number of competitors protects incumbents from supply expansion and preserves positive economic rents rather than causing losses.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Who Captures Long-Run Gains from Cost-Saving Innovation?
questions.prompt_template: An agricultural engineer invents an open-access irrigation technique that lowers every competitive corn farm's minimum Average Total Cost from $4.50 to $3.75 per bushel in a constant-cost industry. How do profits and prices evolve from the short run to the long run?
