hints.text: First consider an early-adopting farm selling at the old $4.50 price, then trace widespread adoption and entry.
In the long run, free entry drives market price to the new, lower min ATC.

options_template.text: Early adopters earn temporary positive economic profits while price remains near $4.50, but widespread adoption and entry shift industry supply rightward until price falls to $3.75 and consumers capture the permanent gains.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Temporary profits reward early cost-cutters, yet competition and entry compel all farms to adopt the lower-cost method (or exit), passing the full $0.75 cost reduction to consumers in the long run.

options_template.text: All farms permanently earn $0.75 per bushel in positive economic profit forever because every farm now has lower costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fallacy of Composition in Entry): Lower costs across the entire industry induce entry and supply expansion that compete market price down to $3.75.

options_template.text: Market price rises above $4.50 because farms must charge more to recover the cost of adopting new irrigation equipment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Direction Inversion): The problem states that the innovation lowers min ATC to $3.75 (already inclusive of equipment costs), pushing long-run price down, not up.

options_template.text: Farms that refuse to adopt the innovation continue breaking even indefinitely alongside adopting farms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (High-Cost Survival Fallacy): Once market price falls to $3.75, non-adopters with min ATC = $4.50 suffer persistent losses ($3.75 < $4.50) and must either adopt or exit.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Critiquing Popular Misinterpretations of Zero Profit
questions.title: Evaluating a Media Claim That Perfect Competition Causes Bankruptcy
questions.prompt_template: A business columnist argues: 'Economic textbooks claim free competition pushes firms to zero economic profit, which proves unregulated competition drives every small business into poverty and bankruptcy.' What is the strongest economic rebuttal to this claim?

hints.text: Clarify the precise definition of zero economic profit versus accounting profit and solvency.
Remember what costs are already subtracted inside Total Economic Cost.

options_template.text: The columnist is right, which is why competitive industries cannot exist without government price floors.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting-Economic Conflation): Competitive industries operate sustainably at zero economic profit without price floors because normal returns are already earned.

options_template.text: Zero economic profit means firms earn zero revenue, but workers still receive wages from fixed costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Revenue Error): Firms in long-run equilibrium collect full revenue P_LR × q_LR covering all explicit expenses plus normal owner returns.

options_template.text: Economic profit only applies to large corporations, whereas small family businesses measure performance strictly by Marginal Cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Firm-Size Scope Error): Economic profit and opportunity cost apply universally to sole proprietorships, family farms, and corporations alike.

options_template.text: Zero economic profit means firms earn a positive normal accounting profit that fully pays all explicit bills plus the owner's full opportunity cost of labor and capital—not poverty or bankruptcy.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because implicit wages and normal returns on capital are already included in economic cost, π_econ = 0 reflects a healthy, sustainable return equal to the owner's next-best alternative.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Long-Run Prices Stay Elevated After a Clean-Tech Demand Boom
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a competitive solar-panel installation industry requires licensed master electricians whose total supply is scarce in the region. Following a permanent surge in household demand for rooftop solar, dozens of new installation firms enter—yet five years later, equilibrium installation prices remain higher than before the boom. Which competitive mechanism explains this outcome?

hints.text: Identify what happens to scarce specialized electrician wages as total industry output expands.
Connect rising specialized input prices to an increasing-cost industry's upward-sloping S_LR.

options_template.text: This is an increasing-cost industry: rapid industry expansion bids up wages for scarce master electricians, shifting every firm's ATC upward so the new zero-profit long-run equilibrium occurs at a permanently higher P_LR.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When industry growth drives up the price of a scarce specialized input, every firm's min ATC rises, tracing an upward-sloping S_LR even with free entry and zero economic profit.

options_template.text: The industry must be a constant-cost market where firms illegally colluded to keep prices above min ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Collusion-Attribution Fallacy): Permanently higher long-run prices after a demand boom occur naturally under competitive free entry whenever specialized input prices rise.

options_template.text: Higher electrician wages shift only Fixed Cost without affecting min ATC or long-run equilibrium price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage-Cost Classification Error): Electrician wages are variable costs that shift MC, AVC, and min ATC upward, directly raising P_LR.

options_template.text: Free entry failed to occur because solar installers are price setters facing vertical demand curves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored-Entry Premise): The scenario explicitly notes that dozens of new firms entered; the higher P_LR reflects rising factor costs, not absence of entry.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Explaining Falling Long-Run Prices During Rapid Industry Expansion
questions.prompt_template: As global demand for a standardized competitive electronic component expands dramatically over a decade, dozens of new assemblers enter the market. Surprisingly, the new long-run equilibrium price settles strictly below its pre-boom level while firms still earn zero economic profit. Which industry structure explains this pattern?

hints.text: Ask what must happen to every firm's minimum Average Total Cost as the entire industry scales up.
Recall the third long-run industry supply case from Section 7.3: external economies in a decreasing-cost industry.

options_template.text: A constant-cost industry where new entrants voluntarily price below min ATC to gain market share.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Below-Cost Pricing Fallacy): Competitive firms cannot survive permanently below min ATC, and in a constant-cost industry P_LR returns exactly to its original level.

options_template.text: A decreasing-cost industry: industry-wide expansion creates external economies (such as cheaper specialized suppliers and shared logistics) that lower input prices and shift each firm's min ATC downward, giving a downward-sloping S_LR.
options_template.feedback: Correct. External economies of scale reduce factor costs as the industry expands, lowering every firm's min ATC so long-run equilibrium settles at a lower price and higher output.

options_template.text: An increasing-cost industry where higher consumer demand shifts market demand downward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Industry-Type & Demand Error): An increasing-cost industry yields a higher long-run price after a demand surge, not a lower one.

options_template.text: A short-run shutdown equilibrium where firms operate permanently below min AVC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shutdown-Equilibrium Confusion): Firms produce zero when P < min AVC and exit in the long run if P < min ATC; lower P_LR is sustainable only because min ATC itself fell.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Applying the Competitive Benchmark to Real-World Markets
questions.title: Distinguishing Near-Competitive Commodity Markets from Differentiated Markets
questions.prompt_template: An economics student compares three real-world markets: (1) unbranded U.S. Grade #2 yellow corn sold at regional grain elevators, (2) patented prescription biologics, and (3) designer athletic sneakers. Which evaluation best aligns with the four assumptions of perfect competition?

hints.text: Test each market against the four assumptions: many small sellers, homogeneous products, perfect information, and free entry/exit.
Remember which real-world sector Section 7.1 highlights as coming closest to the competitive benchmark.

options_template.text: Designer athletic sneakers come closest because millions of consumers buy shoes every year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Large-Market-Equals-Competition Error): Having many buyers is not enough; heavy branding, styling differentiation, and large dominant firms violate homogeneity and price taking.

options_template.text: Patented prescription biologics come closest because clinical trials provide perfect information about drug quality.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Patent-Barrier Oversight): Patents legally block entry and create monopoly power, directly violating free entry and many small sellers.

options_template.text: Unbranded Grade #2 yellow corn comes closest because thousands of small farms sell a standardized homogeneous commodity with transparent spot prices and open entry, whereas patents block entry in biologics and branding differentiates sneakers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Standardized agricultural commodities (corn, wheat, soybeans) approximate all four conditions most closely, whereas patents and brand differentiation depart sharply from price-taking competition.

options_template.text: None of the three can be analyzed with economic models because real-world markets never satisfy every idealized assumption literally.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (All-or-Nothing Model Rejection): Idealized benchmarks remain highly predictive for markets that approximate their assumptions and provide an essential reference point for imperfectly competitive markets.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Normative Welfare Benchmark of Perfect Competition
questions.title: Why Long-Run Competitive Equilibrium Serves as the Efficiency Benchmark
questions.prompt_template: Even though few real-world markets satisfy every assumption of perfect competition strictly, why do economists treat long-run competitive equilibrium (P_LR = MC = min ATC) as the central normative benchmark for evaluating market performance and public policy?

hints.text: Combine both efficiency results achieved simultaneously in long-run competitive equilibrium.
Explain why producing more or less than Q_LR, or producing away from min ATC, leaves society with lower total economic surplus.

options_template.text: Because it maximizes producer profits at the expense of consumer surplus, ensuring businesses grow as rapidly as possible.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Profit-Maximization Benchmark Error): Competitive equilibrium eliminates above-normal economic profit (π = 0) and maximizes total surplus (CS + PS), not firm rents.

options_template.text: Because it guarantees that every consumer pays the lowest possible price of zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Price Misconception): Price equals min ATC = MC > 0, covering the true opportunity cost of scarce resources rather than setting price to zero.

options_template.text: Because it eliminates the need for any property rights, contract enforcement, or market information.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional-Vacuum Error): Well-functioning competitive markets still depend on clear property rights, contract enforcement, and transparent price information.

options_template.text: Because it simultaneously achieves productive efficiency (producing at lowest possible resource cost, P = min ATC) and allocative efficiency (producing every unit whose marginal benefit to consumers exceeds marginal social cost, P = MC), maximizing total surplus.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Achieving both P = min ATC and P = MC means goods are made at minimum average cost and allocated up to the exact margin where willingness to pay equals marginal cost, providing a rigorous welfare yardstick.
